tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: ShowOnboardingRolePicker
tools.description:
Render a clickable role-picker chip row during Cowork onboarding. Call this when asking the user what kind of work they do so they can pick their role and get a matching plugin installed. The role list is hardcoded in the frontend — call with no args.

The call blocks until the user responds. Do NOT call this in normal conversation. Only call this when explicitly helping the user set up Cowork for their role/job function.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

## For Claude: assess all FACTS, rewrite only failing entries

The curator requests a **full assessment pass over FACTS**, not only entries written before the writing guidance. Rewrite entries that fail the checks below; leave passing entries intact. This work follows the positions work and precedes Revival consolidation. It is a proposal for the coordinator's existing record process, not an edit of FACTS or the skills.

### Why the pass includes newer entries

A bounded historical comparison at `origin/main ae2d3dbc5` found:

- `ea4d2f1bf`, October 8: ASD-STE100 enters the skill writer's standing brief.
- `7b434aae5`, October 13: “Write halfway to ASD-STE100” appears in the coordinator's record-writing part. This is the relevant boundary for FACTS.
- `a88e52bf7`, October 13, numbers existing entries. A fact's first appearance with an F-number is not necessarily its creation date.
- Older array-bound material, now F-151, is more focused after consolidation.
- F-261 and F-262, created October 20 in `36d53bdd6`, are useful examples of focused, scoped writing. Their wording was assessed, not their underlying claims independently re-proved.
- F-263 (`5ad4a9957`) and F-264 (`444f37018`) were also created October 20. They mix current behaviour with repair details, counts and historical shorthand, even after changes in the consolidation commit `bd33a2f8b`.

This sample supports uneven application of otherwise useful guidance. It does not establish a general failure of ASD-STE100 or prove that later entries are worse. Age is useful provenance, not a rewrite criterion.

### Entry schema: meaning before format

Retain Markdown and permanent F-identifiers. Refine the existing entry form; do not introduce a database or require every entry to fill repetitive labelled fields.

Each entry should communicate:

1. **Current claim and scope.** What is established, on which execution path, library, call form or other relevant conditions. The title must not imply a broader claim than the body supports.
2. **Consequence and limits.** What a worker can safely conclude or do, with exceptions and unresolved uncertainty kept beside the claim. Include consequences only when they matter.
3. **Evidence and route to detail.** The supporting test, measurement, source reading or report section. Distinguish observed behaviour from code inspection or an inference. A missing automated test is not itself a defect if other evidence is honestly identified.

Keep the source conditions with the claim. Move repair chronology to history and task-specific detail to the cited report. A historical measurement can remain a useful fact if it is explicitly scoped to that measurement; do not mechanically delete every number or past-tense sentence. Link to the owning current count rather than duplicating a count that changes at every landing.

A FACTS entry may record an implementation choice made under a default. It must distinguish that fact from a curator-approved ruling. POSITIONS owns the ruling; history owns its origin.

### Per-entry assessment rubric

Use a temporary assessment table with one row per F-identifier. Mark each criterion **pass**, **fail**, or **unresolved**, with a short reason and a quoted passage for each fail. “Unresolved” means evidence is needed, not that a reviewer may guess.

| Criterion | Pass condition |
|---|---|
| Scope | Title and body agree on the path, conditions and limits; the statement does not generalize beyond its support. |
| Present meaning | The reader can identify the current property, or the explicitly bounded historical observation, without reconstructing a batch's work. |
| Evidence | The stated support can be found and supports the retained claim; uncertainty and the kind of evidence are accurately represented. |
| Comprehension | Given normal language prerequisites, a reader can restate the finding and its consequence. Subjects, referents and technical terms are unambiguous. |
| Ownership | The entry has one independently maintainable subject; unrelated repairs, chronology and duplicated current counts do not obscure it. |
| Consistency | Relevant linked or same-subject entries agree, or their different scopes or unresolved conflict are explicit. |

Do not average these into a score that allows good prose to compensate for an unsupported claim. Scope, evidence and consistency failures block acceptance. Comprehension and ownership failures require a wording or organization correction.

Assign each entry a disposition:

- **Keep:** all applicable checks pass.
- **Reword:** supported meaning is sound, but presentation or scope wording fails.
- **Reorganize:** move detail, merge with an existing owner, or split independently changing claims. Keep conditions and exceptions with their claims.
- **Investigate:** support or consistency is unresolved. Resolve the narrow question before approving new wording; do not silently delete the fact.

Useful completion measures are assessed entries / total entries, counts by disposition, and unresolved failures by criterion. Every entry must have a disposition; every changed entry must be checked again. Report remaining unresolved items explicitly. Character count is a diagnostic, not an acceptance score.

### Run it within the existing process

1. Pin the base and list every F-identifier. Divide the assessment using the coordinator's existing bounded chunks. Calibrate on a few contrasting entries, including a concise one and a dense batch-derived one, before expanding.
2. Read every entry, following its cited evidence as needed to establish the retained claim. Use bounded report sections and related-entry searches. No automatic rerun of experiments or full transcript archaeology; record a narrow evidence gap when those would be needed.
3. Produce the temporary assessment table before rewriting. Do not rewrite passing entries merely to make their surface form uniform.
4. Rewrite or reorganize the failing entries using the existing writer pass. Apply the ASD-STE100-inspired register and the scope-preservation rules. Preserve identifiers and use `record.py` with its history and checks. After splits or merges, reconcile incoming references.
5. Review changed entries against evidence, then use the existing fresh-reader quiz for consequential distinctions. The reader should know ordinary Fortress concepts but not the original conversation. Distinguish a missing prerequisite from defective wording.
6. Recheck affected related entries. Complete the pass with coverage and unresolved-item counts. If main changed during the work, reconcile entries changed since the pinned base rather than overwriting them.
7. Only then use the corrected current record as input to Revival consolidation. Do not copy every fact into Revival.

This is a full entry assessment with targeted evidence review and selective rewriting, not a fresh scientific verification of the entire repository.

### Ownership and minimal instruction changes

The present worker skill already says: “Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.” Keep that division of labour.

- **Rung workers:** provide precise findings, conditions, evidence and implications in their reports and `record.md`. No added prose-polishing workflow.
- **Gather:** incorporate the findings without losing scope or provenance.
- **Record pass:** produce the final readable entries and check their scope, evidence and related statements. The coordinator's instructions assign this to the batch commit stage, and to the coordinator after a lone worker.
- **Coordinator:** own the guidance and verify that the pass occurred. Delegate the writing through the existing process; this need not become another task the coordinator personally performs in full.

Align the rung brief's request for “finished prose” with the worker skill: request complete findings, while making the record pass responsible for final editorial wording.

Put the schema clarification and assessment criteria in `.claude/skills/coordinator/references/record.md`. Ensure the actual batch stage brief carries that guidance, rather than assuming the descriptive skill text alone causes it to happen. The full pass is a one-time repair of the accumulated record; subsequent landings apply the same criteria to new, changed and affected related entries. Do not add another full-record audit after every landing.

For routine acceptance, keep the central question short:

> Can a reader identify what is established, under which conditions, and what it means for the work, without reconstructing what the batch changed?

The corresponding POSITIONS question remains about faithful communication of the curator's ruling. The shared register helps both; their evidence and ownership requirements remain distinct.

## What an entry is

An entry reads on its own. A reader who knows the language, or can look it up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it. The entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.

- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: what is established now, and under which conditions; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; its evidence: the test that gates it, or its source, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred; the decision it builds, by number; and the report section that holds the detail.
- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; where it applies; what it requires of the work; and what is still to build, with its PLAN item. Its "Built." or "Still to build:" line stays in the entry. It lists no FACTS entries: `P-48+` finds them.
- A pointer that stays in an entry carries a few words on what it holds, such as a ledger row's subject. A bare list of numbers goes to the history.
- A handle that only made sense in a past conversation, such as "answer 9", goes to the history.
- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
- A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
- An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own, with its conditions, exceptions and evidence. Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. Before you split, look for an entry that already holds the claim, and move the text there. After a split, grep the record for the old number, and repoint each pointer that meant the claim that moved.
- If several entries together establish a conclusion that workers keep working out again, make it a sentence of the entry that owns its subject, with pointers to the entries it rests on. The pass updates it when one of them changes. Add a new entry only if no entry owns it. Leave a conclusion nobody has checked in its report, out of the entries.
- Keep an entry near 600 characters. This is a check, not a cap, and no reason to split: an entry may pass it if a question below keeps a sentence.
- Write halfway to ASD-STE100.

Ask of each sentence, and act on the answer:

1. Would the reader do otherwise without it? Keep it.
2. Would the reader misread another sentence without it? Keep it.
3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, a correction? Move it to the history.
4. Is it detail needed only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing? Leave it in the report, and name the section.
5. Does another entry or a skill say it? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.
6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count.

Judge a FACTS entry by six checks. Mark each one pass, fail or unresolved, and quote the passage that fails:

- Scope: the title and the text agree on the path, the conditions and the limits, and claim no more than the evidence shows.
- Present meaning: a reader can tell the current property, or a measurement bounded to its day, without rebuilding a batch's work.
- Evidence: the cited support exists and holds the claim.
- Comprehension: a reader can restate the fact and what it means. Subjects, referents and terms are plain.
- Ownership: the entry has one subject. No repair history or copied count hides it.
- Consistency: entries on the same subject agree, or state their different scopes or their conflict.

A fail of scope, evidence or consistency blocks the entry. A fail of comprehension or ownership asks for a rewrite. Give no score: good prose does not make up for an unsupported claim. Then give the entry one disposition:

- keep: every check passes;
- reword: the meaning holds, but the wording or the stated scope fails;
- reorganize: move detail out, merge the entry into its owner, or split it;
- investigate: the support or the consistency is unresolved. Settle that narrow question before any new wording.

Retain Markdown and permanent F-identifiers. Refine the existing entry form; do not introduce a database or require every entry to fill repetitive labelled fields.

Each entry should communicate:

1. **Current claim and scope.** What is established, on which execution path, library, call form or other relevant conditions. The title must not imply a broader claim than the body supports.
2. **Consequence and limits.** What a worker can safely conclude or do, with exceptions and unresolved uncertainty kept beside the claim. Include consequences only when they matter.
3. **Evidence and route to detail.** The supporting test, measurement, source reading or report section. Distinguish observed behaviour from code inspection or an inference. A missing automated test is not itself a defect if other evidence is honestly identified.

Keep the source conditions with the claim. Move repair chronology to history and task-specific detail to the cited report. A historical measurement can remain a useful fact if it is explicitly scoped to that measurement; do not mechanically delete every number or past-tense sentence. Link to the owning current count rather than duplicating a count that changes at every landing.

A FACTS entry may record an implementation choice made under a default. It must distinguish that fact from a curator-approved ruling. POSITIONS owns the ruling; history owns its origin.

### Per-entry assessment rubric

Use a temporary assessment table with one row per F-identifier. Mark each criterion **pass**, **fail**, or **unresolved**, with a short reason and a quoted passage for each fail. “Unresolved” means evidence is needed, not that a reviewer may guess.

| Criterion | Pass condition |
|---|---|
| Scope | Title and body agree on the path, conditions and limits; the statement does not generalize beyond its support. |
| Present meaning | The reader can identify the current property, or the explicitly bounded historical observation, without reconstructing a batch's work. |
| Evidence | The stated support can be found and supports the retained claim; uncertainty and the kind of evidence are accurately represented. |
| Comprehension | Given normal language prerequisites, a reader can restate the finding and its consequence. Subjects, referents and technical terms are unambiguous. |
| Ownership | The entry has one independently maintainable subject; unrelated repairs, chronology and duplicated current counts do not obscure it. |
| Consistency | Relevant linked or same-subject entries agree, or their different scopes or unresolved conflict are explicit. |

Do not average these into a score that allows good prose to compensate for an unsupported claim. Scope, evidence and consistency failures block acceptance. Comprehension and ownership failures require a wording or organization correction.

Assign each entry a disposition:

- **Keep:** all applicable checks pass.
- **Reword:** supported meaning is sound, but presentation or scope wording fails.
- **Reorganize:** move detail, merge with an existing owner, or split independently changing claims. Keep conditions and exceptions with their claims.
- **Investigate:** support or consistency is unresolved. Resolve the narrow question before approving new wording; do not silently delete the fact.

Useful completion measures are assessed entries / total entries, counts by disposition, and unresolved failures by criterion. Every entry must have a disposition; every changed entry must be checked again. Report remaining unresolved items explicitly. Character count is a diagnostic, not an acceptance score.

### Run it within the existing process

1. Pin the base and list every F-identifier. Divide the assessment using the coordinator's existing bounded chunks. Calibrate on a few contrasting entries, including a concise one and a dense batch-derived one, before expanding.
2. Read every entry, following its cited evidence as needed to establish the retained claim. Use bounded report sections and related-entry searches. No automatic rerun of experiments or full transcript archaeology; record a narrow evidence gap when those would be needed.
3. Produce the temporary assessment table before rewriting. Do not rewrite passing entries merely to make their surface form uniform.
4. Rewrite or reorganize the failing entries using the existing writer pass. Apply the ASD-STE100-inspired register and the scope-preservation rules. Preserve identifiers and use `record.py` with its history and checks. After splits or merges, reconcile incoming references.
5. Review changed entries against evidence, then use the existing fresh-reader quiz for consequential distinctions. The reader should know ordinary Fortress concepts but not the original conversation. Distinguish a missing prerequisite from defective wording.
6. Recheck affected related entries. Complete the pass with coverage and unresolved-item counts. If main changed during the work, reconcile entries changed since the pinned base rather than overwriting them.
7. Only then use the corrected current record as input to Revival consolidation. Do not copy every fact into Revival.

This is a full entry assessment with targeted evidence review and selective rewriting, not a fresh scientific verification of the entire repository.

The present worker skill already says: “Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.” Keep that division of labour.

- **Rung workers:** provide precise findings, conditions, evidence and implications in their reports and `record.md`. No added prose-polishing workflow.
- **Gather:** incorporate the findings without losing scope or provenance.
- **Record pass:** produce the final readable entries and check their scope, evidence and related statements. The coordinator's instructions assign this to the batch commit stage, and to the coordinator after a lone worker.
- **Coordinator:** own the guidance and verify that the pass occurred. Delegate the writing through the existing process; this need not become another task the coordinator personally performs in full.

Align the rung brief's request for “finished prose” with the worker skill: request complete findings, while making the record pass responsible for final editorial wording.

Put the schema clarification and assessment criteria in `.claude/skills/coordinator/references/record.md`. Ensure the actual batch stage brief carries that guidance, rather than assuming the descriptive skill text alone causes it to happen. The full pass is a one-time repair of the accumulated record; subsequent landings apply the same criteria to new, changed and affected related entries. Do not add another full-record audit after every landing.

For routine acceptance, keep the central question short:

> Can a reader identify what is established, under which conditions, and what it means for the work, without reconstructing what the batch changed?

The corresponding POSITIONS question remains about faithful communication of the curator's ruling. The shared register helps both; their evidence and ownership requirements remain distinct.

## What an entry is

An entry reads on its own. A reader who knows the language, or can look it up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it. The entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. == explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:45
- P-48 **A type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix takes its bound, never `Bottom`.** The arguments leave a parameter unfixed when it occurs only in the result type; when two arguments meet at it with no narrowest type into which both convert (a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` have one, `ZZ64`, by P-74); or when dispatch, at run time, picks a generic declaration and must choose the instance to run. Its instance is then the intersection of its upper bounds (`Any` if it has none). At checking, that is narrowed by what the call's expected type (P-49 defines it) requires of the declared return type; at run time, by the static type that the checker gave the call. It is never `Bottom`, never the union of the arguments' types, and never the value's type alone. The rule sets the instance, not which declaration runs (P-46). Why: the rule is the team's later word, from the POPL 2019 paper on multiple dispatch, and the curator trusts the team's later work above his own understanding (P-26). The rule changes nothing in microGPT, whose types are concrete. The library keeps the team's declarations of `fail`, `builtinPrimitive` and `List`'s empty comprehension, whose type parameters have no written bound, without the `extends Object` that a batch had added. Under walk, dispatch takes the value's 

POSITIONS.md:47
- P-50 **The body of a `label` expression, and each value that an `exit` gives it, take the expected type of the whole `label`.** A `label` is a named block that code inside it can leave early with `exit`, giving a value with `with`. The specification types a `label` as the union of its body's last expression and the values that its `exit` expressions give. So when a `label` has an expected type, the compiled checker passes it into the body and into each of those values, as it does into each clause of a `typecase`. The specification's inference chapter lists the body and those values as contexts that carry an expected type. P-51 decides the same question for a call written as another call's argument. Built (F-87 lists the checker's contexts that carry an expected type).

13	## 1. What changed
14	
15	The branch was new; nothing was inherited. Four commits: the tests alone (`62a62f94c`, `8166315d4`), the edit (`91ed5d776`), and a follow-up the first distance run asked for (`e995c31c0`). Under Q1 = (a) the rung repaired the Meet Rule pairs one type provides, String's own juxtaposition pair and the declared-type slips, and left every top-level pair of two functional methods to rung O.
16	
17	**Meet Rule pairs, declarations on the meet (P2's devices M and C, and three more):**
18	- `Maybe` declares `map[\G\](f: T->G): Maybe[\G\]` and `ivmap[\G\](f: (ZZ32,T)->G): Maybe[\G\]` (Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:920-921; the component's bodies at Library/FortressLibrary.fss:1441-1444, `cond` over `Just` and `Nothing` as `Condition`'s bodies do). In the api `Maybe` is the first type below both `Condition` and `ZeroIndexed` (Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:917).
19	- `StandardMutableArrayType` declares `copy():T` (Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1466, Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2134), abstract, where `fill` and `tabulate` already meet.
20	- `SimpleMappedSeqGenerator` declares `map`, answering a `SimpleMappedSeqGenerator` over the composed function (Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3554-3555); `SimpleNestedSeqGenerator` declares `map`, answering a `SimpleNestedSeqGenerator` that maps each inner sequential generator, and `nest`, `NestedGenerator`'s body restated (Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3635-3638). The precedent is `SimpleSeqFilterGenerator`'s own `seq` (Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3584).
21	- `String`'s juxtaposition: the three functional methods of `String` (`(a:Any, self)`, `(self, b:String)`, `(self, b:Any)`) become three top-level operators with the same bodies (Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2440-2443, Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4237-4240). Two functional methods with `self` at different positions satisfy neither the Subtype nor the Incompatibility Rule, and the text admits no meet for them (Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:517-523); as top-level functions the Meet Rule for functions is met by `(String, String)` (:411-415 contrasts the two rules).
22	
23	**Slips, each declared type set to what its body answers (P2's S and the rest):**
24	- the api's `AssociativeReduction.lift(r:R)` against `ActualReduction.lift(r:R)` (Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1860); the component's `lift(r:Any)` throughout is unchanged.
25	- the api's `LessThan` and `GreaterThan` `CMP(self, other: LessThan|GreaterThan): TotalComparison`, as the component already declares (Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:139, :150).
26	- `LeftScalarRange.every: BoundedScalarRange`, `LeftScalarRange.atMost` and `RightScalarRange.atMost: FullScalarRange` (Library/RangeInternals.fsi:240, :242, :298; Library/RangeInternals.fss:563, :571, :683), and `RightScalarRange.every: BoundedScalarRange` (Library/RangeInternals.fsi:296, Library/RangeInternals.fss:675), whose body answers a `LeftScalarRange` for a negative stride.
27	- `FilterGenerator.filter: FilterGenerator[\E\]`, the api's own type (Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3568 against Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2101); `MappedGenerator.map: MappedGenerator[\E,G\]` (Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3517). Each had declared an object type that the override in `FilterGenerator2` and `SimpleMappedIndexed` could not answer.

# Concepts for every worker, chunk f6

The entries name these concepts without defining them, since other entries use them too. Each belongs in the `fortress-repo` skill, not in the revival part that is being rewritten.

| Term | Entries | Where to define it | What the definition needs |
|---|---|---|---|
| The interpreter's library, and the compiled library | F-79, F-81 to F-86; most of the section "The checker and the one library" | `fortress-repo` core | The interpreter's library is `Library/` with `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.*`, the library that walk runs and that the switch-over makes the only one; the record also calls it "the one library". The compiled library is the compiler's own small prelude (`CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerLibrary`), which the compiled path uses today. The entries now say "the interpreter's library", as chunk f0 does. |
| The distance, a site of the distance | F-83, F-85; also F-53, F-263, F-264 | `references/compiler.md`, beside the count stage | Chunk f0's `concepts.md` gives the definition. F-53 holds the current value and site list. |
| The Meet Rule, a meet, a functional method | F-76, F-80, F-81, F-82 | `fortress-repo` core, beside multiple dispatch | Two overloads whose parameter types overlap need a declaration at the meet, the intersection of their parameter types (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`). <!-- The FACTS clarity pass, chunk f6, 2026-10-22: F-76 and F-79 to F-87 rewritten from the chunk's assessment, so that a reader without the batches behind them can tell what is established, under which conditions and on what evidence, with each entry's changes of meaning, the source of each sentence, and the points left for the coordinator. -->

# FACTS chunk f6: the rewrite

The base is `main` at `5ca623461`; the assessment read at `a898e1baf`. The assessment keeps F-77 and F-78, so this file holds the other ten: seven to reword, and F-84, F-85 and F-86 to reorganize. A section number is that of the report named. Concepts that the entries use and that every worker needs are in `concepts.md`. `clean.txt` holds the clean entries alone, and `proposals.apply` the lines for `record.py apply`.

The ten entries hold 6,739 characters in the record and about 9,700 here. The growth is the four open items of F-76 spelled out, the limits that F-80 to F-82 and F-84 lacked, and words that say what each pointer holds. F-84 and F-85 are about as long as before, and F-86 is shorter. I could not run `record.py`: this session needs approval for it. So `record.py apply` and `record.py check` on a scratch copy are still to run.

One wording change runs through the chunk: "the one library" becomes "the interpreter's library", as in chunk f0.

## F-76

> - F-76 **The compiled checker accepts the specification's `comprises` example of the Meet Rule by a coverage check used only in overload checking, and types a call whose argument's static type stands between closed traits and their listed types by the intersection of its candidates' return types.** It builds P-60, which reads `comprises` at the level of values: several declarations below two overloads serve as their meet if together they cover it. Open: a family whose declarations have static parameters is refused (row 546), or its call is typed by one candidate chosen by a sort, not by the intersection (row 543, deliberate). On the compiled path, a method call on a value typed by the intersection crashes the code generator (row 540), and a generic declaration instantiated at an intersection type dies as it loads (row 559). The checker checks a `comprises` clause only at the closed trait's immediate subtypes, so a type in another component below a generic subtrait escapes it (row 487). Its verdict on an overload set can depend on the components compiled before it in the same JVM (row 547). Gated by `compiler_tests/*Comprises*` and `*CoverageReturn*`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-return-type-rule/decision-record.md` sections 3 and 4.

Meaning: unchanged. "Between two closed traits" becomes P-60's "between closed traits and their listed types", with "static type" restored, as the assessment asks.

Sources: title, the decision record, sections 3 and 4, and P-60's wording; coverage, P-60; each open item, its gap-ledger row (546, 543, 540, 559, 487, 547); the tests, the assessment's check that they exist.

Not added: the decision record's section 4 types the tie by the intersection only for candidates that fit without coercion. The assessment calls the case narrow, and P-60 states the bound. A worker who needs it follows P-60.

## F-79

> - F-79 **In the interpreter's library, `IntLiteral`, the type that the compiled checker gives an integer numeral, is declared on the model of the compiler's prelude: a sibling of the number types under `Number`, which each integer type, `QQ`, `RR64` and `AnyIntegral` convert from by coercion.** It builds the library half of P-76. Under walk a numeral is still a `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ`, so no numeral reaches these declarations until walk's half is built (F-74). `IntLiteral` declares `Integral[\I\]`'s members, `zero` and `one` itself, since no declaration of `Integral` applies to it, even with coercion. Each integer type declares its own comparisons, `CMP`, `MAXNUM` and `MINNUM`, and a `^` with an `IntLiteral` exponent. Without them, a typed integer with a numeral operand ties between a declaration inherited from a generic trait and the other number types' own. `ZZ32`'s getters `minimum` and `maximum` do not reach a numeral: `(3).minimum` is refused (row 581). Gated by `tests/IntegerOrderNumerals.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-numeral-library/REPORT.md` sections 4 and 6.

Meaning: one correction, as the assessment asks. The old text called `IntLiteral` "the compiler library's", which reads as a type taken from the compiler's prelude. The interpreter's library declares its own, on the prelude's model (P-76; `FortressBuiltin.fsi:179`, `object IntLiteral extends { Number }`). The path is now stated: the compiled checker types the numeral so, and walk does not (P-76, F-74).

Sources: the conversions, `coerce(x: IntLiteral)` in `FortressLibrary.fsi` at `:302`, `:404`, `:443`, `:490`, `:536`, `:594`, `:653`; walk's numeral types, P-76; `IntLiteral`'s own members, the report's section 6 and its judge's reading of `conversions-coercions.tex`; the comparisons and the `^` and why they tie, sections 5 and 6 (`^(self, b:IntLiteral)` at `FortressLibrary.fsi:526`, `:579`, `:637`, `:675`); row 581, the gap ledger, which names `ZZ32`'s getters.

The old sentence "states its comparisons, `CMP`, `MAXNUM`, `MINNUM` and `^` with an `IntLiteral`" could be read as all of them taking an `IntLiteral`. Only `^` does (`FortressLibrary.fsi`); the others are declared at the type's own type, and an `IntLiteral` operand reaches them by coercion (report section 6). The clean text says so.

## F-80

> - F-80 **The compiled checker judges two functional methods of one name, abstract declarations included, by the Meet Rule for Functional Methods in each type that provides both, unless their name is a symbol.** Such a type must provide their meet, compared without the `self` parameter. F-88 says what a type provides. An abstract functional method beside a concrete one with the same parameter type is refused by the No Duplicates Rule. Unchecked: a pair that only an object expression provides (row 570), and every operator whose name is not a word of capitals, such as `+` or `||`, since the checker skips them (row 584; F-245 measures what the skip hides). The checker's overloading memo is keyed on all the inputs of the check, so a pair accepted at the top level is not reused unchecked in a trait that provides it. Gated by `compiler_tests/FunctionalMethodMeet*`, `XXXFunctionalMethodMeetAbstractSibling` and `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleAbstract`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-overloading-checker/REPORT.md` sections 5 and 7; `compile-ladder/rung-checker-abstract-callsite/REPORT.md` section 1.

Meaning: narrower, as the assessment asks. The title and the "Unchecked:" list now name the operators that the checker skips. The memo's consequence is said.

Sources: the skip, row 584's text ("never checks an overloaded operator whose name is not a word of capitals") and the code (`OverloadingChecker.scala:742-746`, `isDeclaredName`; `NodeUtil.validOp` refuses a name of one character, a doubled character such as `||`, `SUM` and `PROD`); the abstract rung left operators as row 584 leaves them (`rung-checker-abstract-callsite/REPORT.md` section 1); the memo, `rung-overloading-checker/REPORT.md` section 7: the memo had answered "valid" for a pair whatever arrows, declarations and kind environment it was checked under, so a pair that the top level accepted was reused in every trait that provides it. I did not write that a verdict no longer depends on order: row 547, open, says that it can depend on the components compiled before it.

## F-81

> - F-81 **In the interpreter's library, each Meet Rule pair inside one type that the compiled checker reads has a declaration on its meet; pairs of operators whose names are symbols, which the checker skips (row 584), are not all met.** `String`'s juxtaposition is three top-level operators, since two functional methods with `self` at different positions have no meet. `String`'s `||`, `|||`, `//` and `///` keep that refused shape (row 585). F-245 gives the other unmet pairs that the skip hides, among them `Indexed`'s three subscripts in 17 types. The same work set some declared types to what their bodies answer, listed in report section 1. Others still differ, such as `__bigOperator2`'s fused branch (F-85). Gated by `tests/LibraryMeetDeclarations.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-meets/REPORT.md` section 1.

Meaning: narrower, as the assessment asks. The meets hold for the pairs that the checker reads. The declared-type clause is limited to the rung's own list of slips.

Sources: the meets and `String`'s juxtaposition, `rung-library-meets/REPORT.md` section 1 (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:517-523`); row 585; F-245 and `perf-probes/symbolic-operators/REPORT.md` section 1.2 for the other pairs; the subscripts still declared so, `FortressLibrary.fsi:1297`, `:1309-1310`, as the assessment read; the fused branch, row 632 and F-85.

## F-82

> - F-82 **In the interpreter's library, the range types declare a method on the meet for each of their Meet Rule pairs that the compiled checker reads, and their declared types match what their bodies answer.** Among the meets are `CAP` at each rank (F-89 holds the ranks' kinds) and `FullRange`'s abstract `IN`, so a numeral `IN` a `#` or `:` range type-checks (row 580). The pairs of `Indexed`'s three subscripts, which the checker skips as operators whose names are symbols (row 584), have no meet in the ranges (F-245). Open library bug: the full sequential ranges' `map` answers a `SimpleMappedSeqIndexed`, which is no `MappedGenerator`, so its `reverse` is `Indexed`'s, and `seq(0:6:2).map(fn x => x + 1).reverse.asString` prints `SimpleReversedIndexed(mapped(seq(1,3,5,7)))`, not `mapped(7,5,3,1)` (row 603). Gated by `tests/RangeDeclarations.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-range-meets/REPORT.md` section 1.

Meaning: narrower, as the assessment asks: the meets hold for the pairs that the checker reads. Row 603 is now called an open library bug, with the value it prints, as the row says.

Sources: the meets, `rung-range-meets/REPORT.md` section 1; row 580 (fixed) and its test; the subscripts, F-245 and its report's section 1.2; row 603's text.

Kept as written: "their declared types match what their bodies answer". The assessment found no fault in it for the range types, and I found no source that narrows it.

## F-83

> - F-83 **In the interpreter's library, the string components `String.fss` and `FlatString.fss` hold no site of the distance, the compiled checker's errors in that library (F-53); their declarations that the checker refused are repaired in forms that the library already uses.** The trait `String` is declared in the `FortressLibrary` api, and has an entry in that component's export error for traits whose declaration differs from the api's: its `extends` clause differs, and the component lacks members that the api lists. That site is `FortressLibrary`'s, and it clears with that export error (`reviews/array-sites-ways.md`, section 4). `FlatString`'s api states its component's header (F-259). Open library bugs: `FlatString.rangeContains` finds only the first occurrence of the character (row 607), and a subscript `:b:c` is completed from the axis's right end, not as `l:b:c` (row 609). 40	Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
41	state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
42	record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
43	store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
44	open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
45	`--from` nor `--note`; for a noted block, no `--note`), a correction that
46	names no block or more than one, two blocks for one entry in one call.
47	Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the record file and its
48	history together.
49	
50	usage: record.py COMMAND [ARGS] [PROVENANCE] [--root DIR]
51	
52	  PROVENANCE: --from PATH#HEADING (repeatable; PATH from the repository root
53	  or from explorations/, HEADING held by exactly one heading of it, as doc:
54	  resolves one), --commit HASH (in HEAD's history), --by WHO, --note WHY.
55	  Each write needs --from or --note.
56	
57	  add F|P --section TITLE FILE   a new entry from FILE's one line, numbered
58	      record.py add F --section 'Landed semantics' new.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The fix' --by coordinator
59	  set N [FILE] [--section TITLE] entry N rewritten from FILE's line, or moved
60	      record.py set F-87 f87.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The question' --note 'cut to the form'
61	  merge N --into M [FILE]        N removed, M rewritten from FILE (or kept),
62	                                 every pointer to N made a pointer to M
63	      record.py merge F-90 --into F-87 f87.md --note 'one fact, two entries'
64	  remove N                       N removed; refused while a pointer to it remains
65	      record.py remove P-131 --note 'evicted to the coordinator skill, references/briefing.md'
66	  note N [--correcting TIME]     a noted block in N's history, N unchanged; needs
67	                                 --note; refused when the history holds it already.
68	                                 TIME: 2026-10-13 19:07Z, or 2nd 2026-10-14 04:41Z
69	      record.py note P-25 --from 'positions-audit/full/evidence/corrections-c1.md#History lines the tool cannot write' --note 'his message behind the text: 2026-09-26T08:01:03.475Z, ...'
70	      record.py note P-7 --correcting '2026-10-13 19:07Z' --commit b87a17de5 --note 'that block names bc8902f47, ...'
71	  apply FILE                     many changes from one file, all or none (below)
72	      record.py apply chunk3.md --by 'consolidation chunk 3'
73	  check [--base COMMIT]          the store's checks; exit 1 on a failure
74	      record.py check --base cc9424c2a
75	
76	An apply file holds, in any order: `## TITLE` or `### TITLE`, the section the
77	new entries below it go to (an existing entry stands under no heading, or
78	under its own section's, or the `## ` one that holds it); entry lines as they
79	should stand, `- F-87 ...`, or `- F-?1 ...` for a new entry, its placeholder
80	replaced by its number everywhere in the file; `move F-87 to SECTION`;
81	`remove F-90`; `merge F-91 into F-87`; `note F-87`, or `note F-87 correcting
82	TIME`, a noted block. Each may be followed by one indented provenance line of
83	its own:
84	`  from: PATH, "HEADING"; commit: HASH; by: WHO; note: WHY`. Blank lines and
85	`<!-- -->` comments are ignored. An entry line equal to the entry is skipped:
86	to add to its history, write `note F-87`. A note whose block the history holds
87	already, all but its time, is skipped too, so a file run twice writes nothing
88	twice. One call writes one block per entry, so an entry is noted, or changed,
89	once in a file.
90	
91	check fails on: an entry line without its number, or a line under an entry
92	that continues it; a number on two lines; a number with no `numbered` or
93	`added` block, or one gone from its file whose last block is not `merged into`
94	or `removed`; a noted block that holds an earlier line, or whose `correcting`
95	names no earlier block of its entry, or more than one; a pointer to no live
96	entry, or quoted words that do not open the target's title; with --base, an
97	entry at COMMIT that is neither its line now nor the earlier line of a block
98	in its history (pointer words refreshed by the tool aside). It reports, without failing: the entries over 600 characters, the
99	entries without a bold title, and the `--from` paths and the report sections
100	an entry cites (`PATH`, "HEADING") that do not resolve.
101	
102	The reads are facts-extract.sh's: `F-87`, `F-87+` (with the entries it points
103	to and that point to it), `history:F-87`, and the title queries, which fall
104	back to the former titles in the history.
105	"""

Readers: Pavol, who decides, and the coordinator. -->
7:Pavol decided on 2026-09-27 that a numeral (an integer written in the program, such as `3`) gets a type of its own, `IntLiteral`, that each number type converts from, in the one library and in walk, the interpreter (POSITIONS 2026-09-27, a numeral's type). Batch N's second run, rung Q, was to build it. Probe Q measured the switch under walk first and found that it changes 59 test verdicts, 24 of them failures that no small device repairs, and asked which shape the rung should take. This judgem
15:- The switch as scoped changes 80 outputs and 59 verdicts over all 440 interpreter tests (`captures/tests-eq1a-compare.txt`, last line: `changed 80 ... verdicts changed 59`).
16:- With the four devices (a numeral at an `AnyIntegral` parameter, a tuple of numerals converted at dispatch, `asif` converting, varargs under rung K's rule), 53 outputs and 28 verdicts change: 4 expected failures turn green (rows 387, 443, 395, 511) and 24 tests that passed fail (`captures/tests-r-compare.txt`, last line; the 24 `VERDICT ... base A pass, edit FAIL` lines).
19:- The `=` devices: `i = 0` for a `ZZ32` `i`, 20K times, takes 5.5 s with the numeral case in `exactValue` against 0.4 s for the control in the same run (13 times), and 2.1 s against 0.4 s with the promoting `=` (5.4 times) (`captures/progs.txt:279-280`, `:298-299`). The compiled library's shape within rung Q's files answers `z = 0` false, silently, for every integer type (`captures/progs.txt:304-308`). Without a device the marker at `exactValue`'s `else` prints 17 times before the program's f
20:- The checker's distance, the count of errors the compiled checker reports on the one library (627 after batch N's first run): 728 on the switch's library copy, 623 once `ZZ32` declares `>`, `>=`, `<=` and `CMP` on itself as `ZZ64` does (`captures/distance-r.txt`, `captures/distance-r1.txt`, `#total` lines). The 101 extra errors are ambiguous coercions between a `ZZ32` and a numeral at those four operators and the generator filters they sit in.
23:- Row 364's mechanism: walk's `narrowest` builds its candidates from each argument value's run-time type and its supertypes (`EvaluatorBase.java:259-260`), so for numeral arguments the implementation class `Int` is a candidate and, being below `ZZ32`, wins. Under the switch that class is `IntLiteral`, and every aggregate of numerals takes it. Read in the source; as the note says.
29:- The compiler library, the team's later model, declares a shift count and an exponent at the type's own width: `ZZ32`'s `LSHIFT(self, other: ZZ32)` and `^(self, other: ZZ32)`, `ZZ64`'s at `ZZ64`, `NN32`'s at `NN32` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:196`, `:259`, `:267`, `:326`, `:385`). A numeral count converts into the receiver's type there. The one library declares the counts `AnyIntegral` by Pavol's decision on row 380 (POSITIONS 2026-09-24), so the compiler library's w
40:The four devices the probe measured repair 33 of the 59 verdicts; the six of the third group would take the walk side of the count to roughly 40 of 59 with an unbuilt device each. The nine of the second group need static types.
46:The specification's design is that numerals are polymorphic and are not converted to any number type until used, "as in common mathematical usage", with the library defining the coercions (`Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:127-148`); the numeral hierarchy itself was never written (`:83-95`, "We need to describe the Numeral type hierarchy"). The team's compiled library built the working version in 2009: `IntLiteral` a sibling under `Number`, a coercion into each integer type. The o
56:The second group of section 3 is the same limit under another name. `<|1, 2, 3|>` at a `List[\ZZ32\]` parameter is typed by the checker from the parameter; walk builds it from the values and gets `List[\IntLiteral\]`. `getDefault(0, 0, 0)` at an instance walk built from `ZZ32` values gets `(Int, Int, Int)`, into which a numeral does not convert. When walk takes the checker's static arguments and coercions, each of these is settled by the same insertion R7 waits for, with nothing built for it 
81:- The devices for rows 395 and 511 (a tuple and a varargs list at dispatch) and `asif` converting as the checker's does. These are walk gaps that exist without the switch, each with a gated test, on no path to microGPT, and they share `bestMatchWithCoercion` with 7b's rung W; they ride here, or with any walk rung that runs after 7b if one comes sooner.

- F-64 **The compiled checker refuses every type that an api declares, trait or object, that extends a trait whose `comprises` clause has `...`, whether the clause lists it or not (row 354).** So the form `comprises { T, ... }` cannot stand in an api that declares `T`. The specification's text allows `...` in an api (`Specification/basic/traits.tex`, "Trait Declarations"). Only a draft note refuses it, and a release build leaves draft notes out. The team's `compiler_tests/XXX3q` and `XXX10p` pin the refusal, and a fix that skips it for a listed type turns them red. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-defects/REPORT.md`, "Defects and their homes".
- F-65 **The checker memoizes `TypeAnalyzer.parents` and `excludesClause` per trait table, and the memo changes no answer.** `FORTRESS_ANALYZER_CLAUSES_CACHE=false` turns it off. By reading, both functions depend only on the table and the type. One differential on climb batch 7C's tree gave the same errors with the memo off and on: 626 at the distance stage and 75 at the count stage. In that measurement the count stage took 1,149 s with the memo off, past its 900-second limit, against 112 s with it on. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-analyzer-memo/REPORT.md`, "Why the memo changes no answer"; `reviews/row-488-probe.md`, "The answer".
- F-66 **The checker-count stage's table, `gate/checker-count.txt`, lands with every batch beside the gate's `summary.txt`.** Its total at the last landed gate is F-53's count. The gate's step 8 compares it with the newest landed table. The total is never red on its own, as P-39 rules, since a fix can raise it and two rungs' changes do not add. The gate is red on a crash line that no rung declared, on a table with no total, and on a stale shadow: the instrumented copy of `StaticChecker` that the stage runs, when it no longer matches the tracked checker. Detail: `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`, "The checker count, and a rung whose test is that stage".
- F-67 **The compiled type checker checks `nat` and `int` static parameters.** A size is a symbol, a literal or an operation on sizes, compared by its written form once numerals are folded (F-146). The checker refuses to infer a `bool`, `dim` or `unit` static argument. Such an argument written out passes the checker, and a `bool` one then stops in code generation (row 406). A call that leaves a size unknown is refused, "Could not infer static argument ... without context"; F-69 gives when an overload set is refused and when it is not. It builds P-40. Gated by `compiler_tests/NatInferredChecker` and its siblings in the report's section 6. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-nat-checker/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-69 **The compiled checker refuses a call whose most specific arm failed only on a size that the call cannot fix, when that arm's parameter type is free of the size.** The message is "Could not infer static argument nat n without context". It drops instead an arm whose unknown size is in its own parameter type (row 400). It lets through a call whose argument's static type lies above the arm's domain, and the compiled run dies reading the size (row 446). It builds P-40. Gated by `compiler_tests/NatKnownSizeArm` and `XXXNatUnknownSize*`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-unknown-size-arm/REPORT.md` section 10.
- F-70 **The compiled checker checks a static argument written at a dotted method call against its parameter's bound, but not one written at a top-level function call.** At a dotted call it puts the written arguments into each bound and refuses a call whose argument misses one, "No such method" (row 651, fixed). At a top-level call it matches kinds only, so `n[\String\]("d")` passes for `n[\T extends Number\](s: String): T` (row 470). Gated by `compiler_tests/MethodStaticArgsBoundNamesOther*`, which cover the dotted call only. Row 470 has no test. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-checker-contexts/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-?1 **No static parameter of the interpreter's library is bounded by `Object`; under walk, an argument whose type is a tuple, `()` or an arrow, at a parameter typed by a type variable bounded by `Object`, stops the program with an `InterpreterBug`, not a type error (row 471).** The library's result-only parameters are unbounded, as P-48 decides (F-84). Six functions of the `FortressLibrary` api write `extends Any`: `cast`, `instanceOf`, `identity`, `shared`, `localize` and `copy`. The specification's examples and the compiler tests write `extends Object`, so they can meet walk's stop; the library's own declarations do not. Row 471 has no test. Evidence: a search of `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, and row 471's probe. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-result-bounds/REPORT.md` section 10.
- F-71 **The compiled checker does not narrow a `typecase` variable in the shorthand form `typecase x of T => ...`, neither path accepts the binding form `typecase x = e of`, and the clause-binding form `x:T =>` runs on both paths.** So write the clause-binding form, as the library does (F-134). The shorthand form runs under walk only. The binding form parses as the equality `x = e`; only the specification's grammar, marked for revision, has it. Row 460 records both refusals, and no test gates them. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-remainder/REPORT.md` section 15.

- F-73 **The compiled checker infers a generic's static arguments with coercion: a type parameter that is the whole type of one parameter, and occurs in no other parameter type, takes the narrowest of its arguments' types, their coercion targets and its bound.** It builds P-74 and P-49. 11	The base is ee1aa1a95. The branch holds one edit of the checker, in `TypeAnalyzer.scala`, from the checker probe's two patches (`explorations/perf-probes/checker-bound-defects/patches/rows-686-687-689-690-normal-form.patch` and `sibling-ground-bound.patch`), applied unchanged (`4356454a2`):
12	
13	- **The normal form** (`normConjunct`, `TypeAnalyzer.scala:708-735`). A closed trait among the conjuncts of an intersection is replaced by the types its `comprises` clause lists that another conjunct excludes only where that conjunct names no type variable and no inference variable (`excludedListed`, `:713-714`). A bound such as `K ∩ R[\T\]` therefore stays the intersection as written, the redundancy branch drops `K` beside a `T` whose bound implies it, and no union the checker builds over such a bound holds a variable. This is the condition under which the POPL 2019 paper proves matching complete (`research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md`, section 6), the type group's late word (P-26). Before the edit, `K ∩ R[\$T\]` became `OR(AND(A,R[$T]),AND(B,R[$T]))`, and the union rule split it before the variable's bound was read (the probe's section 2.2). ## 1. What changed, and why

The base is ee1aa1a95. The branch holds one edit of the checker, in `TypeAnalyzer.scala`, from the checker probe's two patches (`explorations/perf-probes/checker-bound-defects/patches/rows-686-687-689-690-normal-form.patch` and `sibling-ground-bound.patch`), applied unchanged (`4356454a2`):

- **The normal form** (`normConjunct`, `TypeAnalyzer.scala:708-735`). A closed trait among the conjuncts of an intersection is replaced by the types its `comprises` clause lists that another conjunct excludes only where that conjunct names no type variable and no inference variable (`excludedListed`, `:713-714`). A bound such as `K ∩ R[\T\]` therefore stays the intersection as written, the redundancy branch drops `K` beside a `T` whose bound implies it, and no union the checker builds over such a bound holds a variable. This is the condition under which the POPL 2019 paper proves matching complete (`research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md`, section 6), the type group's late word (P-26). Before the edit, `K ∩ R[\$T\]` became `OR(AND(A,R[$T]),AND(B,R[$T]))`, and the union rule split it before the variable's bound was read (the probe's section 2.2). One change clears rows 686, 687, 689 and 690.
- **The union cases** (`pSubInner`, `TypeAnalyzer.scala:165-180`, before the union rule at `:181-182`, both only where the check is not negated). An inference variable below a union takes the union as one upper bound (`:168`), so the inference-variable rule of `fig-subtype.tick` comes before its union rule. A type variable below a union is also tried through its bound, with the type-variable case's history entry (`:171-180`). This clears the ground sibling (711): `g[\T extends { K, Q }\](x: T): T = h(x)` with `trait Q excludes { C }`, where `K ∩ Q` is ground and still expanded to `OR(A,B)`. The solver then takes the intersection of the upper bounds, here the union, which is the bound: P-48.

Row 680's line (`row-680-local-function-group.patch`, `makeTryChecker(this)` to `makeTryChecker(newChecker)` in the `SLetFn` case, `impls/Decls.scala:414`) was applied, built and tested (`3216343f6`), and then held (`e75bb538b`). With it, and with `__bigOperator`'s `body(i)` typed for one run only, the count stage checked the library component whole and took 809 s, past the 690 s that the batch record sets for landing it (section 6). The line is valid and its tests passed on it (section 2). Its tests stay in the tree as expected failures keyed on today's crashes.

- F-90 **In the interpreter's library, several array and matrix declarations and `SUFFIX_SUM` are written so that the compiled checker accepts them: the default vector and matrix and `TransposedMatrix` declare the array family's bound (F-151), `__immutableFactory1` answers an `ImmutableArray1`, `__ImmutableSubArray1` has no `put`, `Matrix`'s `mul` writes its parallel halves as `do … also do … end`, and `TransposedMatrix`'s `add`, `subtract` and `negate` call `Matrix`'s operators.** `SUFFIX_SUM` loops over `seq((0 # (|x| - 1)).reverse)`, since a strided range `a:b:c` is declared `Range[\ZZ32\]`, which is no generator, so the checker refuses `seq(a:b:c)` (row 661, open). The same work built P-53 (`String`'s `left` and `right` answer `Just(c)`) and P-54 (`QQ`'s `ceiling` and `truncate` raise at the infinities and 0/0). Gated by `tests/TransposedMatrixAndFreeze.fss`; the `String` and `QQ` parts by `tests/StringPieces.fss` and `tests/NumberOrderListDeclarations.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-slips/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 6.
- F-220 **The compiled checker accepts `__bigOperator`'s local `body`, typed `body(i: I): L` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss`), so it is no error of the checker count (F-53).** F-228 holds how walk runs it: walk instantiates a big operator's static parameters from a declared type or the elements, not at `BottomType`. Gated under walk by `tests/UnwrittenListMapComprehensionWalk`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-elements/REPORT.md` section 6.
- F-225 **In a self-typed trait with no `comprises` clause, or one that lists only `...`, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as also the implementing type, read from the trait's F-bound; it keeps the signatures plain, and refuses an extender at another type.** It builds P-146. A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`. In a trait whose `comprises` clause lists types, `self` is instead the trait met with the union of those types. An extender at another type is refused, such as `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]`. The rule accepts every self-typed body of the library but `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares instead (P-146); when it landed it cleared 29 sites of the distance, one measurement. Walk has no such rule and loads what it refuses. A compiled body that returns `self` fails verification when the parameter is an object type (row 695). The rule refuses the team demo `trips.fss`'s `generator` (row 710) and `PureList`'s `List` (row 355). Gated by `compiler_tests/SelfType*` and `XXXSelfType*`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-self-type/REPORT.md` sections 1, 2, 4 and 7.
- F-226 **The compiled checker renames an inherited method's own static parameters apart before it uses them: from its trait's in the overloading check, and from the receiver's static arguments at a call.** So `Generator.generate[\R\]`, inherited by `PossibleReductionPair[\R\]`, keeps its own `R` (row 561). At a call, each method that `commonInheritedMethods` returns is instantiated with those of its own static parameters whose names the arguments mention renamed to `name$i`, the form that the checker's messages print. So a method invocation and a call by name inside a trait get the same renaming (row 627). Gated by `compiler_tests/InheritedMethodStaticParamSameName`, `InheritedMethodByNameStaticParamSameName` and `MethodStaticArgReceiverSameName`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-overloading-checker/REPORT.md` section 6 (the overloading check); `compile-ladder/rung-checker-expected-type/REPORT.md` section 1 (the call).
- F-227 **The compiled checker keeps an intersection that names a type or inference variable as written, and reads a variable below a union through the whole union or through its bound.** It expands a closed trait into its listed types only against a conjunct that names no variable (`normConjunct` and `pSubInner` in `scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala`). So a call through a parameter bounded by a closed trait and a bound that excludes a listed type checks, and so does the Return Type Rule's check of an overloading beside such a declaration (rows 686, 687, 689, 690 and 711). A `Box[\T\]` argument under a ground second bound stays refused (row 712). An overloading that the checker accepted through the expansion before this change is now refused, on a question that Appendix I lists as not settled (row 713, contested; `XXXOverloadTwoBoundsClosedTraitExclusion`). Gated by `compiler_tests/*TwoBoundsClosedTrait` and `*TwoGroundBounds*ClosedTrait`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-checker-bounds/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 6.

- F-90 **In the interpreter's library, several array and matrix declarations and `SUFFIX_SUM` are written so that the compiled checker accepts them: the default vector and matrix and `TransposedMatrix` declare the array family's bound (F-151), `__immutableFactory1` answers an `ImmutableArray1`, `__ImmutableSubArray1` has no `put`, `Matrix`'s `mul` writes its parallel halves as `do … also do … end`, and `TransposedMatrix`'s `add`, `subtract` and `negate` call `Matrix`'s operators.** `SUFFIX_SUM` loops over `seq((0 # (|x| - 1)).reverse)`, since a strided range `a:b:c` is declared `Range[\ZZ32\]`, which is no generator, so the checker refuses `seq(a:b:c)` (row 661, open). The same work built P-53 (`String`'s `left` and `right` answer `Just(c)`) and P-54 (`QQ`'s `ceiling` and `truncate` raise at the infinities and 0/0). Gated by `tests/TransposedMatrixAndFreeze.fss`; the `String` and `QQ` parts by `tests/StringPieces.fss` and `tests/NumberOrderListDeclarations.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-slips/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 6.
- F-220 **The compiled checker accepts `__bigOperator`'s local `body`, typed `body(i: I): L` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss`), so it is no error of the checker count (F-53).** F-228 holds how walk runs it: walk instantiates a big operator's static parameters from a declared type or the elements, not at `BottomType`. Gated under walk by `tests/UnwrittenListMapComprehensionWalk`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-elements/REPORT.md` section 6.
- F-225 **In a self-typed trait with no `comprises` clause, or one that lists only `...`, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as also the implementing type, read from the trait's F-bound; it keeps the signatures plain, and refuses an extender at another type.** It builds P-146. A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`. In a trait whose `comprises` clause lists types, `self` is instead the trait met with the union of those types. An extender at another type is refused, such as `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]`. The rule accepts every self-typed body of the library but `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares instead (P-146); when it landed it cleared 29 sites of the distance, one measurement. Walk has no such rule and loads what it refuses. A compiled body that returns `self` fails verification when the parameter is an object type (row 695). The rule refuses the team demo `trips.fss`'s `generator` (row 710) and `PureList`'s `List` (row 355). Gated by `compiler_tests/SelfType*` and `XXXSelfType*`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-self-type/REPORT.md` sections 1, 2, 4 and 7.
- F-226 **The compiled checker renames an inherited method's own static parameters apart before it uses them: from its trait's in the overloading check, and from the receiver's static arguments at a call.** So `Generator.generate[\R\]`, inherited by `PossibleReductionPair[\R\]`, keeps its own `R` (row 561). At a call, each method that `commonInheritedMethods` returns is instantiated with those of its own static parameters whose names the arguments mention renamed to `name$i`, the form that the checker's messages print (row 627). So a method invocation and a call by name inside a trait get the same renaming. Gated by `compiler_tests/InheritedMethodStaticParamSameName`, `InheritedMethodByNameStaticParamSameName` and `MethodStaticArgReceiverSameName`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-overloading-checker/REPORT.md` section 6 (the overloading check); `compile-ladder/rung-checker-expected-type/REPORT.md` section 1 (the call).
- F-227 **The compiled checker keeps an intersection that names a type or inference variable as written, and reads a variable below a union through the whole union or through its bound.** It expands a closed trait into its listed types only against a conjunct that names no variable (`normConjunct` and `pSubInner` in `scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala`). So a call through a parameter bounded by a closed trait and a bound that excludes a listed type checks, and so does the Return Type Rule's check of an overloading beside such a declaration (rows 686, 687, 689, 690 and 711). A `Box[\T\]` argument under a ground second bound stays refused (row 712). An overloading that the checker accepted through the expansion before this change is now refused, on a question that Appendix I lists as not settled (row 713, contested; `XXXOverloadTwoBoundsClosedTraitExclusion`). Gated by `compiler_tests/*TwoBoundsClosedTrait` and `*TwoGroundBounds*ClosedTrait`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-checker-bounds/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 6.
